title: Troubleshooting and Quality Assurance in Hyperpolarized Xenon Magnetic Resonance Imaging: Tools for High-Quality Image Acquisition
protocol: Ensure the 129Xe hyperpolarizer is set up and operational according to guidelines.
Conduct T1 relaxation measurements using NMR on a representative HP 129Xe gas sample.
Keep the HP 129Xe dose bag within the magnetic field of the measurement station until ready for transportation.
Ensure a direct and efficient route from the xenon collection point to the magnet room.
Minimize delays during HP xenon transportation to maintain polarization.
Use a magnetic-shielded suitcase if polarization decreases by 20% or more during transport.
Measure the initial dose equivalent (DE) of the HP 129Xe gas before transportation.
Transport the gas from the measurement station into the magnet bore, then back along the same route to the polarimetry station.
Measure DE again after the round trip to quantify the anticipated signal loss during gas transport.
Place the 129Xe coil correctly in the magnet to ensure proper orientation.
Establish a secure physical connection between the coil plug and the MR system through the designated socket.
Configure the coil software to specify the permissible nuclei as 129Xe.
Divide the well-characterized proton resonance frequency on the MR scanner by 3.61529 to obtain the xenon frequency.
Characterize the coil parameters including maximum transmit amplitude, transmitter reference amplitude, and specific absorption rate (SAR).
Create a thermally polarized 129-xenon phantom.
Connect a glass pressure vessel to a xenon gas-filled bag with an appropriate volume.
Ensure that the bag size is aligned with the vessel's capacity for xenon diffusion and freezing.
Submerge the pressure vessel in a small amount of liquid nitrogen (LN2) to allow xenon diffusion.
Seal the vessel after xenon has formed frozen snow inside.
Allow the sealed vessel to thaw and pressurize it.
Calculate the pressure in the vessel using P = (Vvessel + Vbag)/Vvessel.
Ensure that the gas pressure does not exceed the manufacturer's stated limit.
Place the thermally polarized 129Xe phantom inside the 129Xe coil similarly to how a patient would be placed.
Measure the xenon frequency on the MRI console.
Perform a proton frequency scan as some scanners may require an initial proton frequency localizer.
Use a broadband transmit pulse to excite a high range of frequencies for xenon NMR detection.
Record the detected xenon frequency peak with full precision.
Repeat the experiment at the new frequency using low bandwidth (~1000 Hz) to maximize signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and peak frequency precision.
Save the protocol for future quality control tests.
Prepare a bag of hyperpolarized 129Xe for imaging, ensuring it is free of oxygen.
Measure the 129Xe DE accurately immediately prior to imaging.
Set the test imaging protocol to closely reflect desired in vivo parameters.
Acquire and save the image of the xenon bag as a baseline measure of scanner performance.
Measure and record the SNR of the acquired images alongside all scan parameters and xenon DE.
Perform a full-volume spoiled gradient-echo scan in which the FOV is imaged twice in succession (with FA ≈ 8-10°).
Use identical sequence parameters for both images with no gap between them.
Count the number of phase encode steps, n.
Measure the SNR at the DC offset of the two images, S0 and S1.
Calculate the flip angle map using the measured values.
Provide proper coaching to the subject regarding breath-holding techniques.
Allow the subject to practice the inhalation procedure using a bag of air.
Introduce the HP 129Xe bag after the subject is familiar with the breathing technique.
Instruct the subject to perform a series of breaths with room air.
Have the subject inhale HP 129Xe gas deeply.
Instruct the subject to hold their breath after inhalation.
Initiate the scan according to provided instructions.
Monitor the subject's chest movement closely during the procedure.
Use nose clips to prevent nasal inhalation during breath-holding.
Coach the subject to take deep breaths post-breath-hold to remove xenon from lungs.
Export raw data from the scanner in a list format of complex data.
Reconstruct the image using a fast Fourier transform for rectilinear k-space trajectories.
Carefully brew a precise amount of xenon gas for the control xenon bag, taking note of any nitrogen mixed with it.
Image the xenon bag in the MRI scanner.
Conduct polarization measurements before and after the imaging session.
Use the same imaging sequence for all QC scans.
Note xenon DE values before and after conducting all QC scans.
Create a control noise profile for QC purposes.
Use a 2D GRE sequence with high FOV (400-500 mm).
Include a high Bandwidth per pixel (>50 kHz) in the sequence.
Set the lowest possible repetition time (TR) and echo time (TE).
Acquire the QC for noise profile using a xenon vest or loop coil.
Obtain an image with no sample (HP 129Xe) in the coil to characterize the noise profile.
Examine the acquired noise data, particularly k-space, for non-Gaussian elements.
Create a QQ plot by plotting real/imaginary data against synthesized Gaussian data.
To rule out the scanner as a noise source, acquire images using the standard site protocol with various pulse sequence parameters disabled and electronic components powered off.
If a particular gradient coil is emitting noise, power down the gradients prior to running the scan to examine whether the noise resolves.
Identify irregular noise as high signal 'spikes' in individual k-space pixels with abnormally high or low signals in the real or imaginary channels.
Eliminate potential issues with X, Y, or Z gradients by identifying the direction responsible for the striped pattern.
Perform imaging in different phase encoding orientations including anterior to posterior, head to foot, and left to right.
Systematically examine the resulting images in each orientation to identify which specific gradient direction is contributing to the striped pattern.
Contact the site's clinical engineer to selectively enable and disable individual gradients if needed.
Verify the xenon coil and connection.
Ensure that the xenon coil is selected in the MRI scanner and properly connected.
Carefully inspect the coil connection for any disconnection due to patient movement.
Check if the door of the MRI scanner is securely closed.
Perform spectroscopy on the xenon phantom and verify the Xenon peak height and noise floor from the spectroscopy.
Use a 90° flip angle to ensure the presence of a xenon peak.
Calculate the maximum signal associated with 90° excitation.
Compare the voltage/power with the QC scan results.
Evaluate the xenon coil.
Prepare a small bag of xenon and measure the polarization at the measurement station.
Image the bag with a simple 2D GRE scan on an HP 129Xe bag using parameters including higher flip angle of 90° (adjust pulse duration if necessary).
Use reference voltage based on previous phantom QC, high FOV, and low BW while keeping base resolution low.
Measure the polarization again at the measurement station.
Evaluate for a significant decrease in polarization to suggest potential issues with xenon coil transmitter or amplifier.
Analyze both the k-space and image space data to examine any abnormalities or inconsistencies.
Compare the acquired data with previous scans or reference data to identify potential differences or deviations.
Check for data discretization.
Amplify coil voltages recorded by the scanner spectrometer to ensure full dynamic range.
Discretize the signal temporally according to readout bandwidth.
Digitize analog voltage values into discrete signal bins determined by spectrometer bit depth.
Ensure proper amplification of incoming signal to span the full bit depth.
Avoid performing preparation pulses at the target frequency for hyperpolarized studies.
Calibrate the spectrometer properly to avoid coarse discretization of data.
Monitor population of amplitude bins with digitized data points.
Analyze recorded data for quantization errors and loss of fine detail.
Address artifacts introduced by data discretization affecting SNR.
Ensure accurate analysis of physiological changes is not limited.
